entry.title: SA's Courier Sector Drives EV Transition
entry.summary: For an industry shaped by tight margins, rising fuel costs and a growing e-commerce boom, South Africa's express parcel and courier sector is emerging as one of the more active adopters of electric vehicle technology.
entry.content:
For an industry shaped by tight margins, rising fuel costs and a growing e-commerce boom, South Africa's express parcel and courier sector is emerging as one of the more active adopters of electric vehicle technology.

Discussion at the South African Express Parcel Association's June 2026 Transport Forum revealed an industry that is moving beyond scepticism and beginning to build real operational experience with EVs, even as significant commercial and regulatory hurdles remain.

The conversation was prompted by a question from the floor about the drive towards EV adoption and the practical challenges of implementation in a South African context. The responses from senior figures at two of the world's largest logistics companies painted an honest and instructive picture.

Herman Fenta, managing director of DHL Express South Africa, framed the motivation clearly. "There is a drive to have EV vehicles," he said. "The challenges are the economic viability, the trade-offs between the initial cost and the investment, and then the payback and the return. You have to find that balance between the investment and investing in the future, making sure that as an industry we are more green."

Nelson Tixer of FedEx offered some of the most concrete data to emerge from the discussion. FedEx globally has around eight per cent of its fleet running on electric, but South Africa's operation is substantially ahead of that figure.

"If you look at SA, we run 40% of our PTD EVs," he said. He acknowledged that the capital cost of electric vehicles remains a challenge against conventional petrol or diesel alternatives, but pointed to fuel price trends as a growing counterweight. "Where the fuel price is trending, that trend makes these options more viable as we move along."

Reliability, charging and the road ahead

On reliability, Tixer was broadly positive. "Maintenance cost is extremely low," he said. Charging infrastructure, which has historically been one of the principal concerns for fleet operators considering electrification, is improving through sophisticated remote management systems.

"Some of these service providers who sell these vehicles have got a network of charging stations and they can actually see when your vehicle is potentially in danger of running out of charge. They will reroute those vehicles to the closest station, give it a 30-minute charge, and it negates that risk."

Leisel de Wet of the Africa Supply Chain Excellence Awards brought considerable enthusiasm to the subject. She noted that the EV transition is advancing faster than many in the industry expect, with battery technology becoming lighter, fast-charging infrastructure expanding, and battery-swapping solutions beginning to emerge.

"We are on the doorstep of this transition," she said. "It is maximum five years from now. So it is exciting times." She also pointed to the importance of evaluating total cost of ownership rather than focusing solely on the upfront purchase price, a calculation she suggested increasingly favours electric for last-mile applications.

The panel agreed that short-haul and last-mile delivery represents the most immediate opportunity for EV adoption in South Africa, where predictable routes, depot-based charging and relatively constrained daily distances align well with current battery range capabilities. Long-distance and heavy freight applications face additional regulatory constraints that still need to be resolved at a legislative level.

Route optimisation was raised as a related and complementary tool. Dedric Stopforth of Internet Express pointed out that significant carbon reductions are achievable through smarter routing alone, even before full electrification is in place. "We use a company called Loop and they give us a carbon report on how much we have saved just by route optimisation itself," he said.

The human dimension of EV transition also drew attention. Industry participants noted that electrification demands new skills at every level of fleet operations, from drivers adapting to high-torque, near-silent vehicles to workshop technicians managing high-voltage systems for the first time.

A comprehensive EV management framework is reportedly being developed by the University of Stellenbosch and the Transport Education and Training Authority, expected to cover roles from transitional strategists through to drivers and workshop staff.

entry.title: Europe's EV Progress Undermined By Dirty Hybrid Secret
entry.summary: A major new report from the International Council on Clean Transportation (ICCT) has found that Europe's official car CO₂ figures are painting a far rosier picture of progress than real-world data can support. Drawing on…
entry.content:
A major new report from the International Council on Clean Transportation (ICCT) has found that Europe's official car CO₂ figures are painting a far rosier picture of progress than real-world data can support.

Drawing on onboard fuel consumption monitoring (OBFCM) data from nearly eight million vehicles registered between 2021 and 2023, the research reveals a growing and troubling gap between what cars emit in laboratory tests and what they actually produce on the road.

For conventional internal combustion engine vehicles, including mild and full hybrids, the gap is real and persistent. Real-world CO₂ emissions exceeded official WLTP test values by 18 per cent in 2021 and edged up to 19 per cent by 2023. That is a meaningful discrepancy, yet it pales against what the researchers found when they turned their attention to plug-in hybrid electric vehicles.

The plug-in problem

PHEVs are supposed to bridge the gap between conventional cars and full electric vehicles, offering drivers the flexibility of a combustion engine alongside the ability to run on battery power for shorter journeys. In official tests, that proposition looks compelling. In real-world driving, the picture is altogether different.

The ICCT found that real-world CO₂ emissions from PHEVs were 265 per cent higher than their official WLTP values for cars registered in 2021. By 2023, that figure had ballooned to 401 per cent.

In practical terms, a PHEV registered in 2023 was emitting roughly five times its official CO₂ rating on the road. The core reason is that the WLTP test procedure significantly overestimates how much of the time drivers actually use the electric motor. When the battery runs flat and the combustion engine takes over, emissions climb sharply.

Diesel PHEVs fared worst of all, with a gap of 736 per cent for 2023 registrations. Mercedes-Benz, which accounts for the bulk of diesel PHEVs in the dataset, recorded an average PHEV gap of 614 per cent for that year.

The headline finding of the report is equally sobering at a fleet-wide level. Between 2018 and 2023, official fleet-average CO₂ values fell by 28 per cent. Real-world emissions over the same period dropped by only 15 per cent.

When battery electric vehicles are excluded from the calculation, the picture worsens considerably. Official values for combustion-powered cars fell by 16 per cent, while their real-world emissions declined by just one per cent. Between 2020 and 2023, real-world emissions from vehicles with combustion engines actually increased by two per cent.

The report states clearly that "real-world emission reductions between 2020 and 2023 resulted from the deployment of BEVs rather than efficiency improvements in vehicles with combustion engines." In other words, the progress on paper is largely a function of more battery electric vehicles entering the fleet, rather than cleaner combustion technology.

The ICCT makes three concrete recommendations. First, it calls for the PHEV utility factor curve used in type-approval testing to be reviewed and updated regularly using real-world usage data.

Second, it urges the European Commission to implement a correction mechanism that adjusts manufacturer CO₂ targets based on real-world OBFCM data, with the possibility of this taking effect as early as 2027.

Third, it recommends extending OBFCM data collection requirements to battery electric vehicles under Euro 7, from November 2026, to build a clearer picture of real-world energy consumption and range.

For anyone following the transition to cleaner transport, the report is a timely reminder that laboratory numbers and road reality can diverge sharply. Battery electric vehicles remain the surest route to genuine emissions reductions. PHEVs, however well they perform in tests, are delivering far less on the road than their official figures suggest.

entry.title: NEV Interest Rises As Running Costs Bite
entry.summary: South Africa’s new vehicle market delivered its strongest May performance in 13 years, with growing interest in new energy vehicles becoming a more visible feature of consumer behaviour as buyers weigh fuel prices, finance costs…
entry.content:
South Africa’s new vehicle market delivered its strongest May performance in 13 years, with growing interest in new energy vehicles becoming a more visible feature of consumer behaviour as buyers weigh fuel prices, finance costs and long-term ownership value.

Figures released by naamsa | the Automotive Business Council, show aggregate domestic new vehicle sales rose to 51,071 units in May 2026, up 12.8% from 45,287 units a year earlier. Passenger vehicle sales increased 16.3% to 36,871 units, while light commercial vehicle sales edged up 2.5% to 11,251 units.

The headline numbers point to a market that remains resilient despite a tougher economic backdrop. naamsa said consumers were increasingly focused on affordability, financing costs, fuel efficiency, safety and ownership value. That shift is helping to lift interest in hybrid, plug-in hybrid and battery electric vehicles, even though NEVs still account for a small share of total vehicle sales.

The clearest sign of momentum came in naamsa’s comment that NEV sales for April 2026 gained 120% compared with the same period last year. While the organisation did not provide a May NEV unit total in its release, the signal from dealers is that enquiries are rising as fuel costs and higher interest rates reshape purchase decisions.

Buyers ask sharper questions about electric options

Ryan Seele, an executive member of the National Automobile Dealers Association (NADA), said showroom conversations were changing.

“We are seeing a noticeable increase in discussions around hybrid and electric vehicles. Consumers are asking more informed questions about fuel savings, operating costs and long-term ownership benefits. While new energy vehicles still account for a relatively small portion of overall sales, awareness and consideration levels have increased significantly,” Seele said.

That interest is being driven less by novelty and more by household economics. Fuel prices rose sharply during April and May, contributing to headline inflation of 4.0% year-on-year in April. The SA Reserve Bank then raised the repo rate by 25 basis points to 7.0%, lifting the prime lending rate to 10.50%.

For a market where most vehicles are financed, the higher cost of credit has placed monthly repayments under greater scrutiny. naamsa warned that higher fuel and finance costs create a dual affordability challenge, particularly for first-time buyers, small businesses and transport operators.

Brandon Cohen, national chairperson of NADA, said buyers were taking more time before committing. “Customers are spending more time evaluating options, comparing finance offers and considering total cost of ownership before committing to a purchase. Dealers are having to work harder to convert enquiries into sales, but the demand is there,” Cohen said.

This is the space in which NEVs may gain further traction. Hybrids offer a familiar ownership proposition with lower fuel consumption, while electric vehicles appeal to buyers able to manage charging at home or at work. Price remains a constraint, with dealers reporting strongest demand below R500,000.

For now, NEVs remain a developing part of the market rather than a volume driver. As South Africans become more cost-conscious, fuel-efficient and electrified products are moving from the margins of consideration into mainstream buyer conversations.

entry.title: Maths Behind EV Adoption Questioned
entry.summary: South Africa's electric vehicle (EV) charging infrastructure is improving and the appetite for EV's among fleet operators is genuine. And yet, for the overwhelming majority of South African motorists and logistics companies, the business case…
entry.content:
South Africa's electric vehicle (EV) charging infrastructure is improving and the appetite for EV's among fleet operators is genuine.

And yet, for the overwhelming majority of South African motorists and logistics companies, the business case for battery electric vehicles remains stubbornly difficult to close.

That was the clear-eyed assessment from a recent Isuzu Motors South Africa webinar, in which company president Billy Tom and industry policy expert Justin Barnes examined where new energy vehicles realistically stand in a market shaped by high interest rates, volatile fuel costs and an underdeveloped public charging network.

"Charging infrastructure is a necessary condition. I don't think it's a sufficient condition," Barnes noted. The challenge with battery technology, he argued, runs deeper than whether a driver can find a charge point between Johannesburg and Durban.

According to him, the economics simply do not pencil out for most buyers without government support. "Quite bluntly, I can find very few instances where it makes sense to have a battery electric motor car in South Africa. If there are subsidies, that might change the equation. But at the moment, you've got to care deeply about the environment and have deep pockets to justify battery electric over an ICE equivalent."

The United States experience reinforces his point. Much of Tesla's early momentum was built on a federal subsidy of around $7,500. Buyers who took that deal were, in many cases, making a rational financial decision rather than an environmental one.

Without comparable fiscal support in South Africa, the premium attached to an electric vehicle is difficult to absorb in a market where affordability pressures have been severe for several years running.

The commercial case is more promising, but complexity runs deep

If the passenger-vehicle numbers are discouraging, the commercial picture is more nuanced. 

Tom said that some of his bakery-sector customers have been pushing for compressed natural gas trucks, partly because they operate CNG in their production facilities and can refuel on site, and partly because of the environmental benefits over diesel.

Dual-fuel configurations, running CNG alongside diesel, are currently operating in certain fleets. He did, however, concede that battery-electric trucks have also generated genuine interest. "Two years ago we had a road show where we showed our first battery-electric trucks and tried to gauge appetite from the customers. They've been very keen," Tom said.

That enthusiasm, though, runs into hard physical and financial constraints. Battery weight is a significant issue for freight operators. On a vehicle travelling from Durban to Johannesburg, a heavy battery pack can mean losing a tonne and a half of payload capacity over a 600-kilometre run.

Barnes added that the weight problem reshapes the entire commercial use case. An electric bus running a fixed urban route with a light load can work exceptionally well. But the moment it carries a heavy or variable load over long distances, the battery's energy draw changes its application entirely.

Ultra-fast chargers, capable of recharging in 12 to 15 minutes, could compensate for some of this, but the technology and infrastructure investment required remains substantial.

Tom put the operator's dilemma plainly. "If I'm going to run an electric truck, do I have enough infrastructure from Durban to Joburg where I can fill up my truck? If I don't have, what's the point of doing it?"

There is also the residual value question, which fleet owners in South Africa take extremely seriously. Tom noted that commercial buyers want certainty about what a battery truck will be worth after three years of service, and that answer is still not available with confidence.

The picture that emerged from the discussion is of a transition that is inevitable in direction, uncertain in timing, and highly dependent on policy support that South Africa has yet to provide.

entry.title: iCAUR V23 Brings Retro Flair to SA Roads
entry.summary: A new electric SUV with an unmistakable retro character has arrived in South Africa, as iCAUR — the new-energy vehicle brand operating under the Chery South Africa umbrella — officially launches the V23 in two…
entry.content:
A new electric SUV with an unmistakable retro character has arrived in South Africa, as iCAUR — the new-energy vehicle brand operating under the Chery South Africa umbrella — officially launches the V23 in two derivatives, priced from R519,900.

The V23 slots in just below iCAUR's existing O3T in the brand's local line-up and is designed to broaden the appeal of electric motoring through a combination of distinctive styling, generous standard specification and competitive pricing.

The newcomer arrives in rear-wheel drive 2WD and dual-motor AWD form, targeting buyers who want a practical daily electric SUV without having to make significant compromises on either equipment or personality.

Shannon Gahagan, National Brand and Marketing Manager at iCAUR South Africa, described the V23 as a vehicle with a genuine value proposition. "The 2WD, in particular, delivers an exceptionally strong value proposition, combining distinctive design, practical packaging, generous standard specification and efficient electric performance in a package that makes a compelling case for everyday electric SUV ownership," she said.

A retro blueprint with modern underpinnings

The V23 makes an immediate visual statement through its upright, boxy silhouette, flat bonnet, pronounced wheel arches and robust lower cladding — design cues drawn from classic off-road SUV tradition and executed with a clean, contemporary finish.

Circular headlamp surrounds, slim daytime running lights and a distinctive Lego-inspired brake light mounted on the tailgate reinforce its playful yet purposeful character.

Measuring 4,220 mm in length with a 2,735 mm wheelbase, the V23 is compact on the outside but spacious within. The cabin accommodates five occupants across two rows, with a boot capacity of 372 litres that expands to 994 litres when the rear seats are folded flat.

Under the skin, the 2WD variant draws power from a single rear-mounted electric motor producing 100 kW and 180 N.m of torque, paired with a 59.93 kWh battery offering an NEDC-estimated range of 360 km.

The sprint from standstill to 100 km/h takes 11 seconds. The AWD steps things up with a dual-motor arrangement producing 155 kW and 292 N.m, an enlarged 81.8 kWh battery and an NEDC-estimated range of 430 km, with the century benchmark reached in 7.5 seconds. Both derivatives are capped at a top speed of 140 km/h.

Fast charging capability is a practical highlight. The 2WD can replenish from 20 to 80 per cent in 36 minutes via a DC fast charger, while the AWD requires 42 minutes for the same charge window.

Standard specification across both models is notably comprehensive. A 15.4-inch touchscreen with wireless Apple CarPlay and Android Auto, leather upholstery, ventilated and electrically adjustable front seats, a seven-speaker iCAUR sound system and three USB ports in the front row all feature as standard.

Six airbags, electronic stability control, traction control and brake assist provide the safety foundation on both derivatives, while the AWD adds a 540-degree surround view camera system and a full suite of active driver assistance systems, including adaptive cruise control, automatic emergency braking and lane-keep assist.

The V23 range is backed by an eight-year/200,000 km vehicle warranty, an eight-year/160,000 km power battery warranty for the first registered owner, a five-year/100,000 km service plan and eight years of roadside assistance coverage. The AWD is priced at R669,900.

entry.title: Fuel Prices Increase NEV Interest
entry.summary: South Africa's new-energy vehicle market has shifted from a slow burn to something considerably more urgent. The numbers emerging from April's vehicle sales data suggest a market in genuine transition, and fleet managers who have…
entry.content:
South Africa's new-energy vehicle market has shifted from a slow burn to something considerably more urgent.

The numbers emerging from April's vehicle sales data suggest a market in genuine transition, and fleet managers who have been watching from the sidelines may find the window for careful deliberation is closing faster than anticipated.

April 2026 recorded the highest monthly vehicle sales volumes the country has seen since 2013, with new-energy vehicles posting year-on-year growth of close to 200%. Asian manufacturers now hold four or five positions in the local top-ten sales rankings, introducing competitive price points that are forcing reassessment of total cost of ownership across fleet procurement teams.

It is fair to say the affordability barrier that long kept electric and hybrid vehicles out of serious fleet consideration is, in several segments, beginning to dissolve.

Thembinkosi Pantsi, vice-chairperson of the National Automobile Dealers' Association (NADA) described the shift plainly. "The market is moving," he said, "we're seeing customers who previously wouldn't have considered these vehicles now asking serious questions." His observation reflects a broader sentiment among industry professionals that the conversation has matured from curiosity to commercial evaluation.

The plug-in hybrid electric vehicle is emerging as a pragmatic bridge for fleets with mixed operational profiles. For organisations running vehicles across both urban and long-distance routes, the PHEV offers the fuel savings and emissions benefits of electric driving where charging infrastructure allows, with the reassurance of a combustion engine where it does not.

Several fleet operators are treating PHEVs as a transition vehicle, a means of building organisational familiarity with charging logistics, driver behaviour adaptation and energy cost management before committing to a fully electric fleet strategy.

Rethinking the Residual Value Calculation

However, the single greatest source of hesitation among fleet buyers remains residual value. Fleet procurement decisions are built on predictable disposal outcomes, and the resale market for electric vehicles in South Africa is still finding its feet.

Hideki Machida, Automotive Sector Leader at KPMG offered a candid illustration. "My own EV depreciated to around 35% of its purchase price within two years," he noted, "which is well below what most fleet managers would expect from a comparable ICE vehicle."

His concern is legitimate, and the industry acknowledges it openly. Battery chemistry is also advancing at a pace that risks making today's technology feel dated within a relatively short cycle, and buyer confidence in the downstream market has yet to reach the level that supports robust fleet residual value assumptions.

Until a well-functioning second-hand EV market establishes itself locally, fleet financial models will carry a degree of uncertainty that ICE procurement has not faced in decades.

Machida was careful to present the fuller picture, though. "Battery longevity is actually better than most people think," he said. Evidence from global markets, including reports of high-mileage electric vehicles retaining substantial battery health well beyond 1 000 000 kilometres of operation, suggests that fears about premature battery degradation may be overstated.

Reduced servicing requirements, lower brake wear and the potential for second-life battery applications in stationary energy storage strengthen the financial case when viewed across a longer ownership horizon.

Still, South Africa's policy environment remains a critical variable. Industry voices (like NADA) are pressing government for meaningful purchase incentives and tax structures that would bring new-energy vehicle pricing to a level where fleet operators can build a credible business case without absorbing disproportionate risk.

Several comparable markets have demonstrated that targeted incentives can accelerate fleet electrification substantially within a short period.

What South Africa's April sales data and the growing sophistication of industry debate both suggest is that South Africa's EV transition is a present-tense procurement question. Fleets that begin building operational and financial frameworks now will be considerably better positioned when the market reaches the required inflection point.

entry.title: SA NEV Sales Rise 31.5% in Q1
entry.summary: South Africa's new energy vehicle market posted its strongest quarterly performance in years during the first three months of 2026, with sales climbing 31.5% year on year to 4,585 units, up from 3,487 units recorded…
entry.content:
South Africa's new energy vehicle market posted its strongest quarterly performance in years during the first three months of 2026, with sales climbing 31.5% year on year to 4,585 units, up from 3,487 units recorded in the same period of 2025.

The figures, published in naamsa's first-quarter 2026 quarterly review of business conditions, point to a market that is accelerating well beyond the modest trajectory of previous years.

The surge was driven by a remarkable expansion in plug-in hybrid electric vehicle (PHEV) sales, which jumped from 241 units in the first quarter of 2025 to 1,277 units in the same period of 2026, representing a more than fivefold increase year on year.

Battery-electric vehicle sales also doubled over the same period, rising from 276 units to 544 units. Traditional hybrid sales eased marginally from 2,970 units to 2,764 units, reflecting a market in which consumer preference is gradually shifting towards more fully electrified drivetrains.

Twenty-three industry brands contributed to first-quarter 2026 NEV sales, compared with 30 brands that participated across the full year 2025, suggesting that the broader field of NEV offerings is still consolidating and that further growth can be expected as the year progresses.

For the full year 2025, NEV sales reached 16,716 units, a 7.1% increase on the 15,611 units recorded in 2024. NEVs represented 2.8% of total new vehicle sales in 2025, a modest share that nonetheless reflects steady progress in a market still grappling with affordability constraints, limited public charging infrastructure, and ongoing electricity supply uncertainty.

PHEVs Lead a Decade of Gradual Transformation

The PHEV trajectory over the past decade tells a story of patient but ultimately decisive market development. From a near-absent base between 2005 and 2014, measurable sales began in 2015 with just 124 units. Growth remained irregular through to 2020, with annual volumes rarely exceeding 200 units.

The real inflection point arrived after 2021, when volumes accelerated sharply from 122 units in 2022 to 368 units in 2023, 738 units in 2024, and then to 2,810 units across the full year 2025. The cumulative total of 6,114 PHEVs sold to date underscores the scale of the transition underway.

naamsa's analysis suggests that PHEVs are gaining traction in part because they address consumer anxieties around range and charging availability, offering the reassurance of a conventional fuel backup alongside the efficiency benefits of electrification.

As charging networks mature and grid reliability improves, the expectation within the industry is that fully battery-electric models will capture a growing share of this expanding pool of NEV-ready buyers.

Policy Framework Sets the Stage for Industrial Scale

The South African government has moved to provide a more structured incentive environment for electric vehicle production. President Cyril Ramaphosa signed the Taxation Laws Amendment Bill into law on 24 December 2024, and section 12V of the Income Tax Act took effect on 1 March 2026.

The provision offers a 150% tax deduction on the cost of qualifying parts and assets used by original equipment manufacturers in the production of battery-electric or hydrogen-powered vehicles in South Africa. The incentive applies to equipment and buildings placed in use for the first time between 1 March 2026 and 1 March 2036.

Government has further committed R1 billion over the medium term, with the stated intention of catalysing an additional R30 billion in private-sector investment in the EV value chain. Capital expenditure by the major light vehicle manufacturers reached R7.2 billion in 2025, with an increasing share directed at hybrid and plug-in hybrid model investments.

naamsa has expressed its anticipation of the implementation of the South African Automotive Masterplan 2035 and the Automotive Production Development Programme Phase 2 review, frameworks expected to provide a structured roadmap for NEV production growth and domestic market development.

entry.title: Volvo EX30 Owner Pays 4c per Km
entry.summary: Consumer interest in electric vehicles in South Africa is accelerating, and one of the most compelling data sets presented at a recent industry webinar came not from a research institution but from the personal driving…
entry.content:
Consumer interest in electric vehicles in South Africa is accelerating, and one of the most compelling data sets presented at a recent industry webinar came not from a research institution but from the personal driving record of a Volvo Cars South Africa customer.

Grant Locke, Managing Director of Volvo Car South Africa, used his address at the EE Business Intelligence *webinar in May to share two years of granular charging data from a customer's Volvo EX30, offering private motorists an unusually transparent window into the real cost of everyday electric vehicle ownership in South Africa.

Over a period from March 2024 to March 2026, the customer covered 28,744 kilometres across 188 charging sessions, consuming a total of 4,991 kilowatt-hours of energy. Of those sessions, 179 drew on excess home solar generation or free workplace charging. Just nine sessions were paid for, with total charging costs over the full two-year period amounting to a mere R970.

"The average cost per kilometre for an EV charging at home or at work, assuming 90 percent or more of charging off excess home solar, works out at around four cents per kilometre," Locke told the audience.

By comparison, the same distance driven in a petrol vehicle consuming 7.5 litres per 100 kilometres at R22.40 per litre would have cost an estimated R48,277 in fuel. After deducting the EX30's total charging bill of R970, Locke calculated that the motorist's vehicle had avoided approximately R47,307 in fuel costs over those two years.

Locke's data showed that the EX30 produced a blended emissions intensity of around 106 grams of CO2 per kilometre, against a petrol equivalent of 237.5 grams per kilometre when accounting for fuel extraction and refining. The net result was approximately 3,777 kilograms of CO2 avoided across the two-year period, representing a reduction of roughly 55 percent against a comparable petrol vehicle.

Consumer interest is tracking the numbers

Locke supported the financial case with evidence of rising consumer attention. Google search data for electric car-related keywords in South Africa showed a search index of 37 in the first half of the measured period, rising to 65 in the second half, pointing to a near-doubling of online interest over twelve months. Traffic to the Volvocars.com/za website told a similar story, with BEV product page sessions overtaking petrol model sessions in March and April 2026 for the first time.

On the question of total cost of ownership, Locke acknowledged that South Africa had not yet reached the straightforward position seen in some mature markets. The International Energy Agency's Global EV Outlook 2026 states that electric cars often carry a lower total cost of ownership than ICE vehicles over a vehicle lifetime.

In South Africa, Locke said the picture remained more nuanced. Purchase prices for EVs remain higher than their petrol equivalents, partly as a result of import duties. Operating and maintenance costs are clearly lower, while the residual value question is still developing as the secondhand market matures. Tyre costs and insurance premiums were flagged as areas where EVs may carry a marginal disadvantage at present.

Public charging infrastructure is improving rapidly

Locke also presented data on public charging progress that will reassure private motorists considering longer journeys. Major highway corridors including the N1, N2 and N3 now have charge points spaced within approximately 300 kilometres. In Johannesburg, Cape Town and Durban, a public charge point can be located within 20 kilometres.

Charging speeds are advancing quickly as well. Locke described a first-hand test conducted on 21 May 2026 at the Zero Carbon Charge station at Three Towers on the N3, where a Volvo ES90 charged from 9 percent to 79 percent in just over 20 minutes, achieving a peak charging speed of 321 kilowatts. The session delivered approximately 67 kilowatt-hours and added around 400 kilometres of range.

Rubicon's network data showed that total public charging sessions doubled in 2024 relative to 2023, with early 2026 figures already running 64 percent ahead of the same period last year.

Looking beyond the individual ownership experience, Locke pointed to the emerging capability of bidirectional charging as a development that could fundamentally reshape the relationship between electric vehicles and the home energy system, allowing owners to power appliances, back up the home during outages, and in time, feed surplus energy back into the grid.

*Numerous questions were posed by attendees during the session. You can read those questions — with their respective answers — on this page.

entry.title: Electric Fleets Cross Competitive Cost Thresholds
entry.summary: South African commercial fleet operators that have made the switch to electric vehicles are recording measurable savings across fuel, maintenance and total cost of ownership (TCO), according to data presented by Ndia Magadagela, CEO of…
entry.content:
South African commercial fleet operators that have made the switch to electric vehicles are recording measurable savings across fuel, maintenance and total cost of ownership (TCO), according to data presented by Ndia Magadagela, CEO of Everlectric, at a sector *webinar hosted by EE Business Intelligence.

Drawing on a portfolio of real-world fleet deployments spanning more than 12.5 million kilometres of electric driving across clients including DSV, FedEx, Woolworths, Vodacom and Sanitech, Magadagela's presentation made a detailed financial case for commercial fleet electrification that goes well beyond environmental aspiration.

"Commercial fleets have done the maths," Magadagela told the audience of roughly 850 registered delegates. "They have seen that there are clearer economics. It is cheaper to run. And they have seen that it does not affect their downtime."

Those fleets have collectively saved an estimated 2.75 million kilograms of carbon emissions since deployment began, with Everlectric reporting 100 percent operational availability and zero mechanical downtime across its managed fleet.

Where the savings are found

The core of Magadagela's argument rested on a rigorous TCO analysis comparing the Maxus eDeliver3 electric panel van against the Isuzu D-Max across a modelled five-year lifecycle and 240,000 kilometres. 

On a direct purchase basis, the electric vehicle's TCO came in at R860,000 against R1.26 million for the equivalent ICE vehicle, a saving of approximately 27 percent. On a financed basis, the gap narrowed somewhat, with EV TCO at R1.04 million against R1.28 million for the ICE alternative, still representing a 23 percent advantage.

The figures account for the full cost base, including vehicle price, insurance, fuel versus electricity, service and maintenance, tyre costs, and residual value. Electric vehicles carry a higher upfront capital cost, with the Maxus eDeliver3 coming in at roughly 70 percent above its ICE equivalent before import duties are factored in. The savings, however, accumulate through dramatically lower operating costs.

Electricity costs in the analysis were modelled at R0.45 per kilometre for the EV against R2.41 per kilometre for the diesel vehicle, an efficiency gap of approximately 80 percent in favour of electric. 

Maintenance costs were calculated at R0.41 per kilometre for the EV against R0.76 per kilometre for the ICE vehicle, reflecting the significantly fewer moving parts in an electric powertrain. EVs also demonstrated a superior residual value in the model, with a projected return of R195,000 against R96,000 for the ICE equivalent.

"Additional savings are possible given that EV costing and efficiencies continue to improve," Magadagela noted, "with significant savings expected from 2025 technology."

The crossover point

A critical insight from the presentation was the identification of monthly kilometre thresholds at which operating an electric vehicle becomes cheaper than its diesel counterpart in a fully maintained lease structure. 

For the one-tonne segment, comparing the Maxus eDeliver3 against the Isuzu D-Max, Toyota Hilux and Volkswagen Caddy, the crossover point using 2025 cost data sits at approximately 3,200 kilometres per month. 

For the four-tonne segment, the Maxus eDeliver 75 outperforms all ICE competitors from around 2,500 kilometres per month. In the eight-tonne bracket, the same EV crossover dynamic applies at broadly similar thresholds.

A further comparison between the BYD Dolphin Surf and the Hyundai i10 Cargo, conducted using 2026 data, found a breakeven point of 2,685 kilometres per month, beyond which the electric vehicle is consistently the more affordable option to run.

The data also tested oil price sensitivity on the four-tonne segment. At a diesel price of R22 per litre, the eDeliver 75 becomes cheaper than the average diesel equivalent from around 2,500 kilometres per month. 

At R28 per litre, the crossover arrives earlier; at R35 per litre, the electric advantage widens substantially. Given the global trajectory of liquid fuel prices, Magadagela's sensitivity analysis suggested the EV case would only strengthen over time.

Removing barriers through a service model

Magadagela acknowledged that several structural challenges had historically slowed fleet electrification in South Africa, among them limited model availability, concerns about grid stability, prohibitive upfront capital costs, and the complexity of managing charging infrastructure. 

Everlectric's response has been to structure its offering as an electric vehicle as a service model, delivering the vehicle, dedicated on-site DC fast charging infrastructure, renewable electricity supply, full maintenance, and a cloud-based fleet management application under a single monthly invoice.

"This model allows an electric vehicle user or commercial fleet to use an electric vehicle, have charging infrastructure dedicated to them, have all their maintenance already worked into the solution, and have a driver-facing app that allows them to do their deliveries without the headache of knowing where to charge, when to charge, or when electricity is cheapest," she said.

The approach has proved particularly effective for hub-and-spoke operations, where vehicles return to a central depot for overnight or scheduled charging and predictable daily range requirements reduce range anxiety as a practical concern.

Magadagela said the availability of electric commercial vehicle models had improved considerably in recent years, spanning panel vans, trucks and passenger transport, reducing a barrier that would have prevented fleet adoption only a few years ago.

South Africa's advance in distributed solar generation had further reinforced the business case, with co-located solar and charging infrastructure now common across early adopter sites.

*Numerous questions were posed by attendees during the session. You can read those questions — with their respective answers — on this page.

entry.title: SA Moves to Bolster EV Component Manufacturing

category.term: National Association of Automotive Component and Allied Manufacturers

entry.summary: Trade, industry and competition minister, Parks Tau, has published draft amendments to the Automotive Production and Development Programme (APDP) that would extend government incentives to a broader range of materials used in electric vehicle (EV)…
entry.content:
Trade, industry and competition minister, Parks Tau, has published draft amendments to the Automotive Production and Development Programme (APDP) that would extend government incentives to a broader range of materials used in electric vehicle (EV) manufacturing, with a particular focus on battery production.

The proposals, which are open for public comment, include increased production credits and customs rebates designed to encourage investment in high-value EV components on South African soil.

The changes build on the EV white paper published by the Department of Trade, Industry and Competition (DTIC) several years ago and represent the latest in a series of policy steps taken to develop a domestic new energy vehicle (NEV) ecosystem.

Renai Moothilal, CEO of the National Association of Automotive Component and Allied Manufacturers (NAACAM), welcomed the proposals. "It's a step in the right direction. It's definitely a positive move and building on what was outlined a couple of years ago in the EV white paper published by DTIC," he said.

Regional dimension

Moothilal noted that the incentives would apply across the Southern African Customs Union (SACU), giving the proposals a regional dimension that could have broader industrial significance. "It's applicable across SACU and in some way could give some real impetus to what we talk about when we say regional industrialisation," he said.

The draft amendments follow two earlier policy interventions. An additional cash incentive for NEV components was introduced two years ago, and last year's budget included a 150% accelerated depreciation allowance for electric vehicles produced in South Africa.

The China question

South Africa's efforts to grow its EV manufacturing base come against the backdrop of China's formidable dominance of the global EV market.

Chinese manufacturers, backed by close to two decades of targeted industrial policy and substantial state support, account for more than 60% of EVs sold globally, as well as a commanding share of key component production including batteries.

Moothilal acknowledged the scale of the challenge but argued that South Africa's approach of using tax-based incentives and customs rebates, rather than direct subsidies, was appropriate given the country's fiscal constraints.

He said the goal was to position South Africa and the wider region as investment destinations and technology partners for large Chinese and other international producers.

"The mineral advantages that the region has does give some credence to bringing on board some of the large Chinese component producers," he said, adding that new entrants preparing to enter the South African market were already exploring ways to localise high-value components.

Moothila said more could always be done, but expressed satisfaction that policy was moving forward. "It is good to see some of this coming across the line."
